newsitem.title: ITALY: Millions of dollars spent on World Food Summit.
newsitem.headline: Millions of dollars spent on World Food Summit.

text.p: Well over $10 million was spent in connection with last week's World Food Summit, billed as a no-frills conference, according to figures obtained on Monday from the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
A spokesman for the FAO, responding to enquiries, confirmed that spending from the agency's budget was, as previously stated, around $2 million.

But a further estimated $7 million was contributed by individual governments, international institutions, private foundations and non-governmental organisations and, to a small extent, by private enterprise, the spokesman said.
He told Reuters the money was spent on infrastructure and assistance to developing countries to send delegations to the summit and did not go directly to FAO.
He said the figures could not be put together to arrive at a "cost" for the meeting. "You're not adding like things up," the spokesman said.
Italy had also spent money on security for the five-day summit, disrupted twice by protests, while a number of private companies had provided sponsorship and assistance in kind.
Italian clotheswear company Benetton, computer company Hewlett Packard and Telecom Italia had all provided services or advertising worth about $1 million each, the spokesman said.
He also confirmed in response to questions that FAO had mailed all the names on the Fortune 500 list of the world's top companies to seek funds, though none were forthcoming.
"It was considered a...way of trying to attract some support," the spokesman said. "It wasn't successful."
The food summit, which ended on Sunday, was the last in a series of major U.N. conferences held to discuss how to meet the challenges facing the world on the eve of the 21st century.
Some critics have argued that the money they cost would have been better spent on addressing the problems they discussed.
FAO had $1.271 million in its budget for the summit and $840,000 for staff assignment to the meeting's secretariat.
"The very nature of the way it was run meant it had to be cheaper" than past U.N. conferences, the spokesman said.

This was because the summit was held at the agency's headquarters, cutting out staff travel and other expenses, and because routine FAO meetings rather than special preparatory sessions were used to pave the way for the gathering.

Demonstrators briefly disrupted the final news conference of the summit on Sunday, coming within a few paces of Cuban President Fidel Castro and other leaders to protest that the summit was a sham and that FAO was "fawning" to big business.
"It's hard to see what Telecom Italia is doing for us which means we're selling out to big business," the spokesman said.

The summit agreed a non-binding declaration and plan of action in which governments said they would work to halve the number of people suffering hunger by 2015. The present figure is 840 million people.
